clinicalPearls: Clinical syndrome of gastric acid hypersecretion, severe or refractory peptic ulcer disease and diarrhoea caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumour (gastrinoma)

Suspect it with multiple or recurrent ulcers, ulcers in unusual sites (distal duodenum or jejunum), ulcers refractory to therapy or recurring after Helicobacter eradication, and ulcers accompanied by diarrhoea
Diarrhoea is common and sometimes dominant, and characteristically improves with acid suppression, which helps distinguish it from other secretory diarrhoeas
Diagnosis requires a raised fasting serum gastrin together with demonstrated gastric acid hypersecretion (low gastric pH); a positive secretin stimulation test supports equivocal cases
Proton pump inhibition is the cornerstone of symptom control and is often needed at higher-than-standard doses; it must be interrupted carefully before gastrin testing
Around one-quarter of cases occur within MEN1, so hypercalcaemia and other endocrine features should be actively sought
Gastro-oesophageal reflux and oesophagitis with their complications are common because of the acid load
Complications include ulcer haemorrhage, perforation and stricture, and long-standing untreated disease carries substantial morbidity
reference.pathophysiology: In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, autonomous gastrin secretion from a gastrinoma stimulates enterochromaffin-like and parietal cells, producing sustained hyperchlorhydria. The excess acid overwhelms mucosal defences, causing multiple and refractory peptic ulcers throughout the upper gastrointestinal tract, and inactivates pancreatic lipase while injuring the small bowel mucosa, resulting in maldigestion and secretory diarrhoea. Hypergastrinaemia also drives enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia, which in MEN1 may progress to type 2 gastric neuroendocrine tumours. The tumour itself may be sporadic or arise within MEN1.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of hypergastrinaemia (proton pump inhibitor use, atrophic gastritis, renal failure)
Other secretory diarrhoeas (VIPoma, carcinoid, coeliac disease)
Retained gastric antrum or antral G-cell hyperplasia
Chronic pancreatitis or bile acid diarrhoea
additionalInvestigations: Fasting serum gastrin off acid suppression where safe
Gastric pH or acid output measurement to confirm hypersecretion
Secretin stimulation test in equivocal cases
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy documenting ulcers, prominent gastric folds and reflux disease
Somatostatin receptor PET/CT and cross-sectional imaging to locate and stage the gastrinoma
Serum calcium, PTH and prolactin with MEN1 genetic testing
Chromogranin A for monitoring tumour burden
redFlags: Upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage, perforation or obstruction from ulcer disease
Ulcers refractory despite adequate acid suppression and Helicobacter eradication
Severe dehydration or electrolyte disturbance from high-volume diarrhoea
Hypercalcaemia or other features indicating MEN1
reference.prognosis: With effective proton pump inhibition the acid-related morbidity of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is largely controllable, so long-term prognosis is dictated by the behaviour of the underlying gastrinoma, particularly whether hepatic metastases are present.
pitfalls: Diagnosing on gastrin alone without confirming acid hypersecretion, since proton pump inhibitors raise gastrin physiologically
Under-dosing acid suppression and accepting persistent symptoms
Discontinuing acid suppression abruptly for testing without safeguards, risking ulcer complications
Missing MEN1 and its implications for surgery and family screening
Overlooking that MEN1-related hypercalcaemia can worsen gastrin secretion and acid output
references: ENETS Consensus Guidelines for gastrinoma and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
